title: Saudi Arabia Builds 14-Nation Red Sea Coalition as Houthi Blockade Squeezes Oil Exports; China Blacklists 14 EU Entities in Rare Earth Retaliation; Drone Strike Hits Egyptian LNG Hub
subhead: Saudi Arabia gathered 14 nations into a new maritime defense coalition for the Red Sea after Houthi attacks cut Bab el-Mandeb transit by 30%. China retaliated against EU sanctions by banning rare earth exports to 14 European defense and tech firms. A drone struck Egypt's Damietta LNG terminal, the first attack on Egyptian energy infrastructure in the war.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Forms 14-Nation Red Sea Defense Coalition
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia announced a 14-nation maritime defense coalition to protect shipping around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, after a meeting in Riyadh drew representatives from roughly 50 countries. Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria and several other Arab and African nations affirmed their support, the Saudi Defense Ministry said, according to the Seattle Times and New Arab. The coalition will be headquartered in Saudi Arabia and engage in intelligence sharing, training exercises, and maritime operations. A joint statement described the effort as 'purely defensive and not targeting any country.'

The move comes after the Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi vessels on July 20, and maritime data firm Windward reported that Bab el-Mandeb transits have fallen roughly 30% since the Houthi declaration compared with June, with more than 10 vessels making U-turns in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, according to Ambrey data cited by India Today. Saudi Arabia has also invited European countries and the United States, but some Western officials were reluctant to join without clarity on what membership entails, diplomats told the Seattle Times.

It remains unclear how the new coalition differs from the existing EU Aspides operation protecting Red Sea shipping. The urgency reflects the kingdom's economic vulnerability: Saudi GDP contracted 4.8% in Q2 2026 year-on-year, with the statistics authority citing a sharp decline in oil-related activities, the Seattle Times reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is building a regional security structure for the Red Sea because existing Western-led efforts have failed to protect its oil exports. With Hormuz blocked and Houthi attacks now threatening the Red Sea route too, the kingdom is losing both its main export corridors — and turning to regional partners rather than the US alone for protection.

sections.heading: China Bans Rare Earth Exports to 14 EU Entities in Retaliatory Escalation
sections.body:
China's Ministry of Commerce issued Announcement No. 30 of 2026 on July 24, placing 14 EU-based entities on an Export Control Watchlist, prohibiting Chinese exporters from selling dual-use items to them and barring overseas transfer of Chinese-origin dual-use goods to these targets. The listed entities span eight countries — Germany, France, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands, Czech Republic, Bulgaria, and Lithuania — and hit three sensitive supply chain segments: defense equipment (Rheinmetall AG, TATRA TRUCKS, Cavok UAS), compound semiconductors and infrared optics (InPACT S.A., III-V LAB, Vigo Photonics, Ekspla UAB), and rare earth magnets (Lafert S.p.A., Garnet S.r.l., Antraco Chemie-Handelsgesellschaft mbH), according to SMM/Metal.com analysis.

The action is retaliation for the EU's 21st sanctions package against Russia on July 23, which added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong companies. Combined with 7 European entities restricted in April and 10 US entities named in June, China has now built what SMM calls a dual-targeted 'entity + item' control framework. European terbium prices have already reached $4,150/kg and dysprosium $960/kg, both record highs since 2015, according to Argus Media data cited in the SMM analysis.
sections.whyItMatters: China is no longer just restricting rare earth exports by category — it is targeting specific European companies in the defense, semiconductor, and magnet supply chains. With terbium at $4,150/kg and rising, Europe's defense and energy transition industries face a structural supply crisis that cannot be resolved through alternative sourcing for 3-5 years.

sections.heading: Drone Strike Hits Egyptian LNG Terminal at Damietta
sections.body:
A drone caused the fire that engulfed two gas vessels at Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta on July 29, the Egyptian cabinet confirmed on July 30, according to Reuters. The targeted vessels included the US-owned Energos Winter LNG floating storage unit and the Greek-flagged GasLog Salem, CryptoBriefing reported. No casualties were reported, and Egypt's Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said the country had secured alternative energy supplies sufficient to meet national demand.

The strike raises direct concerns about the nearby Suez Canal and SUMED pipeline, both critical corridors for Middle Eastern oil exports to Europe. Reuters reported that the attack renewed 'energy security concerns about the nearby Suez Canal and a related pipeline.' No group has claimed responsibility, and the Houthis have denied involvement. Egypt, a close US ally, is one of the few regional states that has avoided direct military involvement in the Iran war.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first attack on Egyptian energy infrastructure in the current war. Damietta hosts one of the Mediterranean's key LNG import and regasification hubs. If drone strikes become a recurring threat at Egypt's Mediterranean ports, the Suez Canal — the other remaining major oil transit route — becomes a target too, further squeezing global shipping options.

sections.heading: Oil Posts 21% Monthly Gain as War Disruptions Erase Diplomatic Lulls
sections.body:
Brent crude rose 0.7% to $89.64/bbl and WTI gained 0.6% to $84.06/bbl in Asian trading on July 31, both benchmarks on track for roughly 21% monthly gains — their strongest since March, Econotimes and NewsBytes reported. The surge follows a volatile week: Brent had spiked back above $90 on Wednesday after Iran's missile attack on US forces in Jordan and the US retaliation, then eased after Saudi Arabia announced the Red Sea coalition. CNBC reported Brent closed Thursday at $89.03/bbl, down nearly 2%, while WTI settled at $83.59/bbl.

US commercial crude inventories fell by 7.2 million barrels to 404.5 million in the week ending July 24, the lowest since 2018, per EIA data cited by Econotimes. Refining margins for gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel remain near record highs after attacks on refineries across the Middle East and Russia. Jay Hatfield of Infrastructure Capital Management told NewsBytes he expects oil to stay in an $80-$100 range, and the IMF warned that sustained instability could tip the global economy into recession.
sections.whyItMatters: Oil's 21% July gain reflects a market that has stopped pricing in diplomatic off-ramps and is now structurally pricing war disruption. Inventories at 2018 lows, refining margins at records, and multiple chokepoints under fire mean every lull is bought and every escalation drives new highs.

sections.heading: US Sanctions IRGC-Backed Maritime Extortion Scheme Using Bitcoin
sections.body:
The US Treasury's OFAC designated two IRGC-backed firms — HormuzSafe and Persian Gulf Marine Insurance — for forcing commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz to purchase mandatory maritime 'insurance' that was in reality a coercion and extortion scheme. HormuzSafe accepted Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency payments, making it one of the first documented cases of a state-backed entity using crypto to collect maritime extortion revenue.

The scheme operated by compelling ship operators to pay for 'insurance' coverage before allowing safe transit through Iranian-controlled waters, effectively monetizing the blockade Iran has imposed on the Strait of Hormuz. The Treasury designation freezes any US-based assets and prohibits transactions with the two firms.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is not just blocking Hormuz militarily — it is commercializing the blockade through a state-run extortion scheme that accepts cryptocurrency. This is a new form of chokepoint monetization that blends maritime coercion with digital finance, and the US designation signals that Washington sees crypto-facilitated sanctions evasion as a front in the economic war.

sections.heading: Ukraine Hits Four Russian Tankers, CPC Terminal Shut Again
sections.body:
Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces struck four tankers in the Black and Azov seas, expanding a maritime campaign that has now targeted 205 Russian cargo vessels since July 6, commander Robert Brovdi reported on July 30, according to United24 Media. The strikes were part of Operation MoLoChKa, Ukraine's sustained campaign against vessels supporting Russian oil exports and military logistics. The Marshall Islands-flagged tanker NISSOS SIFNOS was hit, sparking a fire on its cargo deck and forcing oil-loading operations to stop at the CPC terminal, according to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium's Telegram channel.

Reuters reported that Kazakhstan's main oil export terminal at Novorossiysk closed for the third time this month after Ukrainian drones hit two vessels at or near the terminal. The terminal handles over 80% of Kazakhstan's crude exports. A second tanker, the Isle of Man-flagged MARATHI, was struck roughly seven miles from the offshore loading terminal while approaching to load oil.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian-linked shipping is now a systematic blockade of its own — 205 vessels hit in 24 days. The CPC terminal's third closure this month shows how effectively Ukraine can shut down the Black Sea export route for both Russia and Kazakhstan, removing roughly 1.3 million bpd from global supply each time it closes.

sections.heading: White Mesa Mill Breaks Ground on Heavy Rare Earth Processing in Utah
sections.body:
Energy Fuels' White Mesa Mill in San Juan County, Utah, broke ground on an expansion that will bring heavy rare earth element processing to commercial scale for the first time in the United States, the Deseret News reported. The mill currently produces about 1,000 tons per year of lighter rare earth elements in its pilot stage. The new facility will process heavy rare earths — dysprosium, terbium, and other elements essential for defense, automotive, robotics, and data center applications.

The expansion is backed by a conditional $725 million loan from the US Department of War and is expected to be operational by July 2027, with a second phase completed by 2029. Energy Fuels CEO Ross Bhappu said the mill is 'in the sweet spot between uranium and rare earth minerals.' The US currently has only three rare earth processing facilities, and China controls roughly 90% of global rare earth processing capacity.
sections.whyItMatters: The White Mesa expansion is the most tangible US effort to date to break China's rare earth processing monopoly — but it will not produce until mid-2027 at earliest, and at a fraction of China's scale. With China now targeting specific EU defense firms for export bans, every Western rare earth project becomes more strategically valuable and more urgent.

bottomLine: Saudi Arabia is building a 14-nation Red Sea coalition because neither US-led patrols nor the EU's Aspides mission has kept Houthi attacks from cutting Bab el-Mandeb traffic by 30% — and because its GDP just contracted 4.8% in Q2. China's retaliatory export controls on 14 EU entities mark a shift from broad category bans to targeting specific defense and tech firms, pushing terbium to $4,150/kg and threatening Europe's defense supply chain. A drone strike on Egypt's Damietta LNG port extends the war's geography to the Mediterranean, raising fears for the Suez Canal. Oil posted its strongest monthly gain since March at 21%, with inventories at 2018 lows. Ukraine hit 205 Russian-linked vessels in 24 days and shut the CPC terminal for the third time this month. Each of these developments points in the same direction: chokepoints are being weaponized, monetized, or disrupted faster than the diplomatic architecture can adapt.
sources: Seattle Times, New Arab, India Today, CNBC, Econotimes, NewsBytes, Reuters, SMM/Metal.com, Argus Media, CryptoBriefing, United24 Media, Deseret News, Caspian Pipeline Consortium Telegram, EIA, US Treasury OFAC, Ambrey, Windward
